item.title: China seeks to bring archaeology closer to public
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04
BEIJING, Nov. 4 (Xinhua) -- China is seeking to bring archaeology closer to the public, with a new five-year plan setting out priorities for research, international cooperation and the wider presentation of archaeological findings. China now has 65 national archaeological site parks, which are increasingly becoming visitor destinations. Visits to these parks rose from 20.97 million in 2021 to 97.74 million in 2025, with a total of 303 million visits over the five-year period. A museum built largely underground at the Dahecun National Archaeological Site Park in Zhengzhou, central China's Henan Province, displays more than 1,500 artifacts illustrating the history of a Neolithic settlement dating back about 7,000 years. In Luoyang, also in Henan, several major archaeological sites spanning different historical periods have become cultural landmarks woven into the modern cityscape. "Archaeological work is moving from a niche specialty toward broader public engagement," said Zhang Lei, head of the archaeology department of the National Cultural Heritage Administration (NCHA). The administration has issued a plan for archaeological work during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). It calls for deeper research into the origins and development of Chinese civilization, stronger international cooperation, greater use of technology and wider dissemination of archaeological findings. China will continue the Chinese Civilization Origins Project and major projects under the Chinese Archaeology Program, with research focusing on the origins of civilization and the formation of early states. Archaeological work will be deepened at major sites, including Erlitou, the Yin Ruins and Sanxingdui. The plan also calls for research tracing the development of civilization along the Yangtze River, further study of human origins and evolution in East Asia, and more archaeological work on maritime cultural heritage in the South China Sea and East China Sea. International cooperation is another priority. China will carry out joint archaeological projects with foreign partners, focusing on Belt and Road partner countries, and develop five to 10 model projects for Sino-foreign archaeological cooperation. The plan also calls for closer collaboration between archaeology and the natural sciences, humanities and social sciences. China will strengthen archaeological laboratories, develop and apply key technologies, and advance research in digital and intelligent archaeology. Training the next generation of archaeologists will be essential to these efforts. Shen Ruiwen, head of Peking University's School of Archaeology and Museology, said the school will support the compilation of textbooks on Chinese archaeology, promote standardized training bases and strengthen a training model combining classroom instruction, fieldwork and laboratory research. It will also expand targeted training in lesser-known academic fields. Zhang Zhiguo, deputy director of the NCHA's National Center for Archaeology, said the center would continue to strengthen its laboratories and scientific archaeology teams, promote interdisciplinary research and deepen international cooperation. It will also upgrade equipment, develop technologies and improve management to support archaeological work. Beyond research itself, the plan emphasizes the interpretation, use and wider dissemination of archaeological findings. Authorities will advance the publication of major archaeological reports, improve the management of archaeological archives and promote regular procedures for the transfer of excavated cultural relics. Efforts will also be made to expand educational activities at archaeological sites and public archaeology programs, while diversifying the ways in which findings are explained and shared. The aim is to ensure archaeological discoveries contribute to the public's knowledge of history and cultural heritage, as well as to academic understanding of China's past. ■

item.title: On Mount Tai, a tough test for China's robots
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04
JINAN, Nov. 4 (Xinhua) -- Carrying eggs, instant noodles and bottled water on their backs, robotic dogs began climbing Mount Tai in east China's Shandong Province on Monday, setting off at two-minute intervals on a challenging 3.9-kilometer route involving more than 3,100 steps. The route took them along steep slopes and uneven stone steps, some barely wide enough for half an adult foot. The climb was part of a robot competition that brought together companies, universities and research teams from across China. For their developers, the mountain offered a chance to test technologies in a demanding real-world setting and explore their potential applications in everyday life. The competition assessed not only climbing speed, but also the ability to transport cargo safely. Items included fragile goods, such as eggs and watermelons, as well as irregularly shaped objects, such as thermos flasks. Damage to delicate cargo would cost points. "Eggs are fragile. We have to consider how to carry them steadily up the mountain while minimizing breakage," said Li Jinxiang, a marketing manager at GENISOM AI, one of the participating manufacturers. The task was familiar on Mount Tai, where human porters have long carried supplies up steep stone steps for tourists. Robotic dogs have already begun taking on some of that work, hauling supplies uphill and garbage downhill. But the terrain remains difficult even for machines built to negotiate rough ground. Chen Xiyun, marketing manager at Unitree Robotics, said the mountain's steps varied widely in height and width. Rain made them slippery, while steep slopes and crowds of tourists added to the challenge. Such conditions, he said, made Mount Tai an ideal testing ground for robots intended for practical use. While robotic dogs are being tested for carrying heavy loads, wearable robots are finding another use: helping people walk. The competition also included an exoskeleton-assisted climbing event to assess how well wearable devices could reduce the physical effort of climbing the mountain. Similar technology is finding applications in rehabilitation, outdoor recreation and fitness. MileBot, a robotics company in east China's Anhui Province, has developed a walking-assistance exoskeleton weighing just 1.8 kilograms, and about 2 kilograms with its battery. The company initially manufactured medical devices, and its exoskeleton products have been used in several hospitals for lower-limb rehabilitation. It has since expanded into industrial robotics and wearable smart devices. Dai Hui, the company's regional manager for east China, said the device could recognize different walking patterns, including the shorter steps taken by some older people, and adjust its assistance accordingly. It can also provide assistance to either leg, a feature Dai said could help improve walking patterns in people with partial paralysis following a stroke. Another setting adds resistance, making walking on level ground feel more like climbing uphill. Dai said the mode was intended for physical training. China is seeking to expand such applications under its 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030). But the competition on Mount Tai also showed the challenges that remain. Some robotic dogs stumbled or bumped into walls. Several humanoid robots lost their balance, with some falling shortly after setting off. Others still depended heavily on human operators. Liu Wenqiang, vice president of China Center for Information Industry Development, said testing robots in real environments helped manufacturers collect data to improve their products. The data collected on Mount Tai could also help developers prepare robots for other tasks. Wang Yani, a brand strategy executive at Universal Ubiquitous AI Co., Ltd., said the data could support future applications in power facility inspections, security patrols and emergency rescue operations. "We hope robots can help people with work that is dirty, tiring and physically demanding," she said. ■

item.title: Democrats projected to win U.S. Congress in midterm elections
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04
WASHINGTON, Nov. 4 (Xinhua) -- Democrats are projected to flip control of the U.S. Senate after winning several key races in battleground states, securing control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, election forecasting agency Decision Desk HQ reported late Tuesday. Before the midterms, Republicans held 218 seats in the House of Representatives, compared with 214 for Democrats. The chamber also had one independent member and two vacancies, one in a Republican-held district and the other in a Democratic-held district, following the resignations of their respective representatives in 2026. With 218 seats required for a majority, Democrats needed a net gain of just three seats to regain control of the House. The latest projections from NBC indicated that Democrats could win more than 250 seats, marking a major political turnaround in the House. Several media outlets described the outcome as a "blue wave" or even a "blue tsunami." Before the Senate elections, Republicans held a 53-47 majority over Democrats. Democrats needed a net gain of four seats to reach the 51-seat threshold for a majority. As votes were counted throughout election night, U.S. media outlets projected Democratic victories in several states, including North Carolina, South Carolina, Texas, Kansas, Ohio and Maine. Notably, South Carolina, Texas and Kansas are all traditionally Republican strongholds, having voted for Donald Trump in each of the past three presidential elections. Texas Democratic Senate candidate and state Representative James Talarico is projected to defeat Republican candidate and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, becoming the first Democrat since 1988 to win a U.S. Senate seat in the state. Democrat Gina Hinojosa is also projected to win the Texas governor's race and become the state's first Democratic governor in more than 30 years. In Kansas, Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton is projected to defeat Republican incumbent Senator Roger Marshall, becoming the first Democrat since 1932 to win a Senate election in the midwestern state. The emergence of these "blue sprouts" in traditionally Republican strongholds has attracted widespread attention. Commenting on the midterm election results reported so far, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries called the outcome a "victory for America" in a social media post on election night. With Democrats poised to take control of the House, Jeffries is set to make history as the first Black speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives. Politico reported that the long-feared "blue wave" had begun sweeping across the country, with Republicans bracing for what could be a crushing defeat in the midterm elections. "This is the worst electoral defeat in my lifetime and likely in history," one GOP operative was quoted as saying. Multiple opinion polls offer insight into the public sentiment behind the "blue wave." Preliminary exit poll results released by CNN showed widespread voter dissatisfaction with the state of the nation, the economy and President Donald Trump's job performance. According to the poll, roughly three-quarters of voters nationwide said they were dissatisfied with or felt even more negatively about the direction of the country. The Associated Press reported that voters had punished Trump, with Republicans paying a steep price across nearly every front. The party's electoral defeat appeared to represent a direct repudiation of Trump by voters. According to the report, Trump had repeatedly demanded loyalty from Republicans across the party, but led them into the midterm elections burdened by his persistently low approval ratings, an unpopular war with Iran, and surging living costs that had left millions of Americans deeply frustrated. The report also noted that, since World War II, control of both chambers of Congress has switched from one party to the other in the same midterm election only three times: 1946, 1994 and 2006. People close to Trump are blaming the Iran war, with some White House officials and Republican allies saying the Iran war was misguided, and the midterm elections would have looked very different if the conflict wrapped up months ago, The Wall Street Journal reported. Trump, meanwhile, admitted that the war in Iran was partially to blame for widespread Republican losses in the elections. But he maintained that he didn't regret launching the war earlier this year. "Iran was a piece of it," he said in a phone interview with The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday night. He rejected the notion that the results were a rebuke of his presidency, even as Republicans lost in deep-red states such as Kansas, South Carolina and Texas, and his poll numbers have dropped significantly across many states. "It was a point in time, and I wasn't on the ballot," he said in the interview. "The biggest issue is that I wasn't on the ballot." In Iran, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the results of the U.S. midterm elections showed that the American people said "no" to war. "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," he said in a post on X. "If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare." The House of Representatives plays a key role in setting the legislative agenda, overseeing federal spending, and conducting congressional investigations and oversight. The Senate, meanwhile, has the power to confirm presidential nominees for key positions, including federal judges and Cabinet officials. Major legislation involving the federal budget and appropriations, as well as defense and foreign policy, must pass both chambers of Congress. With Democrats on track to take control of both chambers of Congress, the Trump administration could face significant legislative and political constraints in advancing its agenda over the next two years. ■

item.title: China's space station exposure platform delivers original results: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04
BEIJING, Nov. 4 (Xinhua) -- China has completed multiple batches of in-orbit experiments on material and biological samples using its space station's extravehicular exposure platform, achieving a number of original results, according to Pang Zhihao, a chief science communication expert on space exploration technology. The space station is currently carrying out its fourth round of extravehicular exposure experiments, covering eight scientific projects and 26 sample units, with exposure periods of one to two years. "Extravehicular exposure experiments place material and biological samples on platforms outside the space station, exposing them directly to the real space environment," said Pang in an interview with Science and Technology Daily. The samples are subjected to high vacuum, atomic oxygen erosion, cosmic radiation, sharp temperature fluctuations and micrometeoroid impacts. After a period of in-orbit testing, they are retrieved by astronauts or a robotic arm and returned to Earth for analysis, Pang revealed. According to the expert, in materials research, China has completed the world's first in-orbit verification of the space stability of a stainless magnesium alloy, confirming its advantages of being both lightweight and radiation-resistant. It also conducted solid-liquid composite lubrication and gel lubrication friction tests outside the station, achieving near-zero wear. Meanwhile, simulated lunar soil bricks remained intact after one year of exposure to extreme space conditions, verifying the feasibility of using such materials for lunar surface construction, Pang said. In the field of biology, China conducted extravehicular exposure experiments on extremophile microorganisms and nematodes, and data on radiation damage and life tolerance were obtained, providing a basis for the exploration of extraterrestrial life and the assessment of radiation risks to astronauts. "The platform has completed multiple batches of sample retrieval and established an evaluation system for space service of materials, providing key data for material selection and protection design for crewed lunar missions and deep-space exploration," Pang noted. He added that many results can also be applied to high-end ground equipment, such as components for aviation, nuclear power and precision transmission, thus improving corrosion, wear and radiation resistance. China's space station, Tiangong, which means Heavenly Palace, has now entered an era of long-term human habitation. The Shenzhou-23 spacecraft was launched on May 24 this year, meaning its crew has now been in orbit for over five months. One crew member is scheduled to conduct a one-year in-orbit stay, while the country's 2030 crewed moon landing mission is advancing steadily. ■

item.title: 7th World Media Summit to kick off in Beijing to boost media cooperation in intelligent age
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04
BEIJING, Nov. 4 (Xinhua) -- The 7th World Media Summit, which is co-hosted by Xinhua News Agency and the People's Government of Beijing Municipality, is to be held from Nov. 5 to 9 in Beijing. According to the summit secretariat, under the theme "Media in the Intelligent Age: From Consensus to Action", the summit will bring together nearly 500 delegates from nearly 330 mainstream media outlets, think tanks, government departments and international organizations from 112 countries and regions around the world. Delegates will exchange views on topics including "AI for all and the transformation of global media," "media dialogue and cooperation for a safer world," "AI-enabled communication for expanding exchanges among civilizations," "AI+ and the future of global communication governance" and "the Beijing approach: decoding Chinese modernization." They will also tour Beijing on the sidelines of the summit. The mechanism of the World Media Summit was initiated in 2009 and is an important global platform for high-end media exchange and cooperation. ■

item.title: China's services trade maintains brisk growth amid push for new drivers, opening up
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04
BEIJING, Nov. 4 (Xinhua) -- China's trade in services maintained brisk growth in the first nine months of 2026 as the country moved to foster new drivers of foreign trade and promote high-standard opening up. Services imports and exports totaled 5.77 trillion yuan (about 858.89 billion U.S. dollars) in the Jan.-Sept. period, up 8.5 percent year on year, according to the Ministry of Commerce. Exports rose 14.8 percent while imports grew 4.8 percent, leaving a services trade deficit of 1.23 trillion yuan. This performance was buoyed by a surge in transport services and steady gains in knowledge-intensive sectors. Transport services led all categories with growth of 33.9 percent in this period. Knowledge-intensive services, which accounted for 43.9 percent of total services trade, expanded steadily by 7.4 percent. These figures underscore a broader shift in China's trade structure as the country moves toward a more consumption- and innovation-driven economy. Experts say the development of services trade is significant for building new competitive advantages in international trade, fostering a more open economy, and supporting high-quality development. Policy support has been strengthened. The 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for vigorously developing services trade, while the 2026 government work report vows to improve national standards for the service sector and cultivate the "China Services" brand. In April, the Ministry of Commerce launched a plan to develop national demonstration zones for the services trade in 16 cities, including Beijing, Tianjin and Shanghai, as well as Hainan Province, with the goal of cultivating key services industry clusters and significantly improving the level of services trade liberalization by 2035. China's growing services trade carries global significance as well. Li Bin, deputy head of the State Administration of Foreign Exchange, said China's services imports reached more than 620 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, covering travel, intellectual property, transport and business services, making China the world's second-largest importer of services. China's steady growth in services imports has strongly supported the development of global services trade and effectively promoted employment and growth in other economies, Li noted. ■

item.title: Xi Focus: Unlocking a vast market for the world
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04
SHANGHAI, Nov. 4 (Xinhua) -- After a journey of more than two months across continents and oceans, machinery from WFL Millturn Technologies cleared customs in Shanghai last month for this year's China International Import Expo (CIIE), carrying the Austrian manufacturer's hopes of expanding further into Chinese and wider Asia-Pacific markets. "I don't see any good reason why we will not be successful in China in the upcoming decades," said WFL Managing Director Stefan Hackl. His company will make a double debut: its first appearance at the import expo after more than 20 years in the Chinese market, and the Asian debut of its brand-new machine tool. The company's confidence is rooted in part in the vision behind the CIIE, an initiative championed by Chinese President Xi Jinping, who has personally planned and steered its development. Designed to give overseas businesses greater access to the vast and growing Chinese market, the expo has increasingly turned China's development into opportunities for the world. Now in its ninth year, the CIIE has become a regular fixture on the global trade calendar. Running from Nov. 5 to 10, the expo will bring together 4,142 overseas exhibitors, including more than 2,000 first-time participants like WFL. In the weeks leading up to the expo, shipments from around the world continued to arrive in Shanghai, bringing in a diverse range of products, from Peruvian bananas and French tires to Australian coffee and Kazakh ice cream, all ready to meet buyers at the event. As the world's first national-level exhibition dedicated to imports, the CIIE offers a compelling response to rising protectionism and trade barriers. Rather than viewing trade as a competition for a limited share of global demand, it seeks to make the world economic pie bigger by creating opportunities for businesses and economies to grow together. "Our aim is to turn the China market into a market for the world, a market shared by all, and a market accessible to all," Xi has said. "This way, we will be able to bring more positive energy to the global community." A PROMISE KEPT In his keynote speech at the opening ceremony of the first CIIE in 2018, Xi said the expo is "an important decision made by China to pursue a new round of high-level opening-up, and is China's major initiative to still widen market access to the rest of the world." "China's initiative to expand imports is not a choice of expediency. It is a future-oriented step taken to embrace the world and promote common development," Xi said, pledging that the event would be held annually and "feature good performance, good results and continued success in the years to come." Eight years on, the CIIE has grown into a premier global platform for trade, investment and cultural exchanges, connecting businesses, innovators and consumers from around the world. The promise of an annual expo with lasting results has been borne out by its growth. Past editions have drawn more than 180 countries, regions and international organizations and seen more than 3,400 new products, technologies and services make their debut, while cumulative intended deals have exceeded 580 billion U.S. dollars, according to the organizer. "The CIIE is far more than a trade show," said Jérôme Vanachter, president of Lesaffre Greater China. The French yeast maker is back for a ninth consecutive edition this year. Calling the expo a "market-intelligence hub," Vanachter said the CIIE helps turn market insights into products. Past expos have also seen Xi announce a series of opening-up measures, including advancing the development of pilot free trade zones and the Hainan Free Trade Port (FTP), continuously trimming the negative lists for foreign investment, and expanding the opening of telecommunications, healthcare and other services. These pledges were followed by concrete actions. In November 2024, China removed the last two manufacturing-related restrictions from its national negative list for foreign investment. Last December, the Hainan FTP launched island-wide special customs operations, a milestone in China's drive for high-standard opening-up. "Today, the CIIE has become a showcase of China's new development paradigm, a platform for high-standard opening-up, and a public good for the whole world," Xi said at the fifth edition of the event in 2022. The role of the CIIE in China's opening-up agenda is expected to continue in the years ahead. In its five-year development blueprint for the 2026-2030 period, the country has called for expanding imports and continuing to hold the CIIE and other major trade fairs, including the Canton Fair in south China, while strengthening trade-promotion platforms. A MARKET SHARED BY ALL "Economic globalization represents the trend of history," Xi said at the second CIIE in 2019, likening it to the world's great rivers -- the Yangtze, the Nile, the Amazon and the Danube, which all "surge forward in relentless flow, and nothing can stop their mighty movement." China has been translating this vision into action by opening wider. Quality products from an increasing number of countries are finding a foothold in the Chinese market, generating profits for businesses, wages for workers and tax revenues in their home countries. For 17 consecutive years, China has remained the world's second-largest importer. Also in the first three quarters of 2026, the country's imports rose 22.3 percent year on year, significantly outpacing export growth. "The vastly huge China market is the most promising in the world," Xi noted at the third CIIE in 2020, citing the country's huge population and vast middle-income group. The country's retail sales of consumer goods surpassed 50 trillion yuan (about 7.44 trillion U.S. dollars) for the first time last year, and are expected to grow by another 10 trillion yuan over the next five years. The appeal of the Chinese market is reflected in the growing participation of global businesses in the CIIE, which has attracted a record number of more than 300 Fortune Global 500 companies and industry leaders this year. In terms of exhibition space, U.S. exhibitors lead for the eighth consecutive year, occupying more than 50,000 square meters, while companies from Germany, the United Kingdom and France also rank among the top participants. Over 480 products are set to make their global, Asian or China debut at the event, the highest number in history, underscoring the Chinese market's growing role as a launchpad for global innovation. Under Xi's leadership, China has also sought to make the opportunities offered by its market more accessible to developing countries. For years, the CIIE has provided free exhibition booths to exhibitors from the world's least developed countries. This year, according to the organizer, the exhibition area for African businesses is set to increase steadily, while the space allocated for free booths for the least developed countries will expand by 17 percent. An official delegation from Cote d'Ivoire will make its first appearance at the CIIE's business exhibition this year, showcasing cocoa, coffee, cashews and kola nuts. In May, a zero-tariff policy took effect on imports from all 53 African countries with which China has diplomatic relations. "We are very happy to participate for the first time," said Rami Koné, an official with the country's export agency. "This will be a good opportunity to showcase Cote d'Ivoire to the world." "Of the problems confronting the world economy, none can be resolved by a single country alone," Xi once said. "We must all put the common good of humanity first rather than place one's own interest above the common interest of all." As Xi has pledged, China will continue to open its arms to the world, offering countries greater opportunities for market access, investment and growth. "Together, we can achieve development for all," he has said. ■

item.title: From ancient wisdom to modern engineering: How China manages the Yellow River
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03
From an ancient vision to modern engineering, China is using precisely controlled water and sediment regulation to tackle sediment buildup in its mother river, the Yellow River. Through 33 coordinated reservoir operations, the average riverbed elevation of the main channel in the lower reaches has been reduced by 3.1 meters, helping improve the river's long-term health and flood prevention.■
